aido-data-pipelines-etl-elt-batch-stream.core: Data pipelines are AI's supply chain. ELT (load raw, transform in the warehouse) has largely replaced ETL. Batch engines like Spark (optimised by Catalyst) handle large bounded data, stream engines like Flink (windows, state, watermarks) and Kafka Streams handle continuous data, and you choose by latency, complexity and operational capacity.

first_principles.problem: Scattered, stale or unreliable data starves analytics and AI.
truths: Data must move and be shaped.
Time and order are hard in streams.

analogy.title: A logistics network
analogy.story: Bulk freight on schedules (batch), express couriers for urgent items (streaming) and warehouses that repackage goods on demand (ELT).
analogy.breaks: Pipelines need quality checks and lineage, or bad data flows quickly everywhere.

example.title: A modern data platform
flow: Raw to lake → dbt ELT models

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Fresh and historical data for every consumer.

example.outcome: reliable data flow for analytics and AI.

check.q: What are watermarks used for in stream processing?
check.a: Tracking event-time progress so windows can close correctly despite out-of-order events.

aido-vector-databases-rag.core: Vector databases give AI long-term memory: embeddings place meaning in vector space, RAG retrieves relevant chunks into prompts like an open-book test, ANN indexes (IVF partitions, HNSW graphs) make search fast at scale, and the database is chosen pragmatically, from pgvector to purpose-built engines.

first_principles.problem: LLMs lack your private, current knowledge and hallucinate without grounding.

analogy.title: A library with a semantic catalogue
analogy.story: Books are shelved by meaning, a fast catalogue finds related pages, and the reader answers questions using them.
analogy.breaks: RAG needs evaluation (retrieval recall, answer faithfulness) to be trustworthy.

example.title: An internal knowledge assistant
flow: pgvector HNSW index with team filters

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Trusted answers grounded in company docs.

check.q: What are the four steps of a RAG request?
check.a: Embed the question, retrieve relevant chunks, augment the prompt with them, and generate the answer.

aido-model-serving-inference.core: Model serving is ML's last mile: expose models through standard inference APIs, choose serving tools by stage (FastAPI → Triton/KServe → vLLM for LLMs), version models with lineage in a registry, and validate new versions with shadow mode, canaries and A/B tests.

first_principles.problem: Models stuck in notebooks deliver no value, and careless deployments cause silent damage.

analogy.title: Bringing a new dish to a restaurant chain
analogy.story: Standard ordering (API), professional kitchens (servers), recipe records (registry), and trial runs before the full menu launch (shadow, canary, A/B).
analogy.breaks: After launch, monitor for data and prediction drift.

check.q: What's the recommended validation sequence for a new model?
check.a: Shadow mode, then a canary release, then an A/B test before full rollout.

aido-llm-ops-hosting-economics-adapters.core: LLM Ops tames giant models: quantise to fit VRAM, serve efficiently with vLLM's PagedAttention and continuous batching, design around token economics and context windows, and customise with LoRA/QLoRA adapters rather than costly full fine-tuning.

first_principles.problem: LLMs strain GPU memory, budgets and latency, and naive approaches fail at scale.
truths: Memory scales with parameters and KV cache.

analogy.title: Running a fleet of huge cargo ships
analogy.story: Lighter cargo (quantisation), efficient docking (vLLM), fuel budgets (tokens), careful loading (context) and modular containers (adapters).
analogy.breaks: Hosted APIs may be cheaper below certain scales, so compare TCO.

example.title: A self-hosted assistant stack
flow: Small model for routing easy queries

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A 5x cheaper cost per conversation than the naive design.

check.q: Name two techniques that reduce LLM serving memory.
check.a: Weight quantisation (e.g. INT4) and paged KV-cache management (PagedAttention).

aido-compute-optimization-gpu-numa.core: Compute optimisation squeezes value from expensive GPUs: slice them with MIG for small workloads, train on spot instances with thorough checkpointing, and remove hidden bottlenecks like NUMA misplacement so GPUs stay fed.

first_principles.problem: Idle, oversized or starved GPUs waste most of the AI budget.
truths: Many jobs are small or interruptible.

analogy.title: Running a factory with one costly machine
analogy.story: Share it across products, run it on cheap power at night, save work in progress and place materials next to it.
analogy.breaks: Measure before optimising: profile GPU utilisation, memory and input pipelines.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: More AI for the same budget.

check.q: Name two ways to reduce GPU cost for AI workloads.
check.a: For example, partitioning GPUs with MIG for small workloads and running checkpointed training on spot instances.

aido-ai-hardware-topology.core: AI hardware topology is the plumbing of intelligence: HBM feeds GPU cores at TB/s, workloads are memory-bound or compute-bound, NVLink/NVSwitch connect GPUs within a node, InfiniBand or RoCE connect nodes, and all-reduce performance (helped by GPUDirect RDMA) determines how well training scales.

first_principles.problem: Fast GPUs wait on slow memory and networks, wasting expensive compute.

analogy.title: A city's water system
analogy.story: Large mains (HBM), local pipes between houses (NVLink), aqueducts between towns (InfiniBand), and valves that bypass treatment plants when possible (GPUDirect).
analogy.breaks: Topology choices cost a lot, so match them to the scale of training actually planned.

example.title: Designing a training cluster

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Near-linear scaling to hundreds of GPUs.

example.outcome: clusters whose plumbing matches their compute.

check.q: Which interconnect handles GPU-to-GPU communication inside a node?
check.a: NVLink, often with NVSwitch for all-to-all full-bandwidth connections.

aido-distributed-training-primitives.core: Distributed training breaks through two walls: data parallelism (DDP) speeds up models that fit, tensor and pipeline parallelism split models that don't, ZeRO/FSDP removes memory redundancy, and 3D parallelism maps each strategy onto the right tier of the hardware hierarchy.

first_principles.problem: Training is too slow on one GPU, or the model doesn't fit at all.
truths: Work and state can be partitioned.
Each split has a communication cost.

analogy.title: Organising a massive construction programme
analogy.story: More crews in parallel, splitting each building's work, staging floors, sharing tools rather than duplicating them, and coordinating it all.
analogy.breaks: Efficiency falls with communication, so measure the scaling and tune it.

example.title: Scaling from 1 to 512 GPUs

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Training time from months to days.

example.outcome: training that scales with model and data size.

check.q: What problem does ZeRO solve that plain DDP has?
check.a: Redundant storage of optimizer states, gradients and parameters on every GPU.

aido-feature-stores.core: Feature stores are the supply chain for AI: one definition per feature, offline stores for history and online stores for millisecond serving, point-in-time joins that prevent leakage, and a registry for discovery and reuse, which defeats training-serving skew.

first_principles.problem: Duplicated, inconsistent feature logic causes silent model failures and wasted effort.

analogy.title: A central ingredient supply for a restaurant chain
analogy.story: Standard recipes, a long-term pantry and a fast prep station, ingredients dated correctly, and a catalogue chefs can browse.
analogy.breaks: It adds infrastructure, which is worth it once several models share features.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Consistent features and faster model development.

check.q: Which feature store capability prevents data leakage during training?
check.a: Point-in-time (as-of) joins that use only feature values available at each label's timestamp.

aido-data-contracts-quality.core: Trust in pipelines comes from data contracts (agreed schemas, semantics and SLAs enforced by schema registries), data tests (expectations with Great Expectations, Soda or dbt that block bad batches) and drift monitoring (data and concept drift) that catches silent degradation.

first_principles.problem: Bad data flows silently into dashboards and models because pipelines succeed even when the data is wrong.
truths: Data is an interface between teams.
Correctness isn't the same as successful execution.

analogy.title: Food safety in a supply chain
analogy.story: Supplier agreements (contracts), batch inspections (tests) and ongoing sampling for changing conditions (drift).
analogy.breaks: Quality is a shared responsibility, so producers must own their contracts.

example.title: A trusted pipeline
flow: Soda checks before publishing to warehouse
Evidently drift reports on model features

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Bad data is caught at the source.

example.outcome: data that teams and models can trust.

check.q: Which layer catches breaking schema changes before data is produced?
check.a: A schema registry enforcing compatibility rules defined in the data contract.

aido-vector-index-internals.core: Vector indexes make similarity search fast by giving up exactness: HNSW navigates a layered graph, IVF scans only nearby clusters, and PQ compresses vectors so billions fit in memory. Every choice trades recall, latency and memory.

first_principles.problem: Exact nearest-neighbour search over billions of high-dimensional embeddings is far too slow and memory-hungry.
truths: High dimensions defeat classic spatial trees.
Memory is the binding constraint at scale.

analogy.title: A huge library with smart navigation
analogy.story: Signposted routes (graph), labelled sections (clusters) and compact index cards (PQ) get you to the right book fast.
analogy.breaks: Libraries return exact books, while ANN occasionally misses a true neighbour.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Combine techniques to meet all three constraints.

points: HNSW, IVF and PQ are the core ideas.

check.q: What three quantities does every vector index trade off?

aido-storage-for-ai.core: AI storage exists to keep GPUs fed: parallel filesystems and object stores supply bandwidth, sharding defeats the small-file problem, GPUDirect removes copies, and streaming decouples dataset size from local disk.

first_principles.problem: Expensive GPUs sit idle because data can't arrive fast enough.
truths: GPUs consume data faster than naive storage delivers.

analogy.title: A supply chain feeding a factory line
analogy.story: Big trucks, many loading bays, containers instead of loose items and direct delivery to the line.
analogy.breaks: A factory can stockpile; GPU memory is small, so data must stream continuously.

example.title: Fixing a starved cluster
flow: Stream from S3 with NVMe cache

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Fix the data path before scaling compute.

example.outcome: GPUs doing work instead of waiting.

check.q: Name two causes of GPU starvation.
check.a: Small-file metadata overhead and insufficient storage bandwidth (or CPU-bound decoding).

aido-notebooks-jupyter-colab.core: Notebooks are interactive documents where a browser frontend drives a stateful kernel. They excel at exploration and visual debugging, but hidden state and poor testability mean stable code should graduate to modules.

first_principles.problem: Data work needs fast iteration and visual feedback, but ad-hoc notebooks become unreproducible production liabilities.
truths: Kernel state can diverge from visible code.

analogy.title: A lab notebook that becomes a published paper
analogy.story: Messy experiments first, then a clean, reproducible method others can follow.
analogy.breaks: Papers are static; production code keeps evolving.

check.q: Where does notebook code actually execute?
check.a: In the kernel process, which may be local or remote, not in the browser.

aido-data-lineage-cataloging.core: A data catalog makes datasets discoverable and trustworthy through metadata (owners, schemas, descriptions, quality), and lineage maps how data flows so you can debug upstream and assess downstream impact. Metadata arrives by crawling (pull) and by events (push).

first_principles.problem: Data nobody can find, trust or safely change.

analogy.title: A library index plus citation graph
analogy.story: The index helps you find books; citations show which work built on which.
analogy.breaks: Library metadata is curated by hand; data metadata must be largely automated.

example.title: Investigating a bad dashboard number
flow: Upstream lineage → a dbt model → a source table
Catalog shows owner and failed quality check

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Lineage and catalog together turn hours of hunting into minutes.

example.outcome: fast root cause with clear ownership.

check.q: How do catalog and lineage complement each other?
check.a: The catalog says what data is and who owns it; lineage says where it came from and what depends on it.

aido-federated-learning.core: Federated Learning trains a shared model across many data holders without moving their data: send the model out, train locally, average updates (FedAvg). Real deployments must handle non-IID clients and protect updates with secure aggregation and differential privacy.

first_principles.problem: Valuable data can't be centralised because of privacy, law or bandwidth.
truths: Models move more cheaply than data.

analogy.title: A travelling teacher learning from many classrooms
analogy.story: The teacher visits each class, learns from it, and shares only general lessons, never students' names.
analogy.breaks: Even 'general lessons' can reveal specifics without formal privacy tools.

example.title: A federated keyboard model
flow: Phones train overnight on charge + Wi-Fi

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Privacy and systems constraints shape the algorithm.

check.q: Name the two main privacy techniques used with FL.

aido-ray-distributed-computing.core: Ray turns Python functions into distributed tasks and classes into stateful actors, linked by futures and a shared-memory object store. High-level libraries (Data, Train, Tune, Serve) build on these primitives to run the whole ML lifecycle on one cluster.

first_principles.problem: Python can't natively scale beyond one machine's cores.
truths: The GIL and single-machine limits cap Python.
Most distributed work is tasks or stateful services.

analogy.title: A city-wide dispatch system
analogy.story: Couriers (tasks), specialist desks (actors) and local depots (object stores) coordinated by dispatch.
analogy.breaks: Unlike a city, a Ray cluster can grow and shrink in minutes with autoscaling.

example.title: An LLM batch inference job
flow: Ray Data reads Parquet from S3
map_batches over a GPU actor pool

check.q: What's the difference between a Ray task and actor?
check.a: A task is a stateless function call; an actor is a stateful process whose methods run serially.

aido-slurm-hpc.core: Slurm is the batch scheduler of supercomputers: a central controller queues jobs and allocates whole sets of nodes and GPUs fairly, users declare resources in sbatch scripts, and long jobs survive failures through checkpointing and requeue.

first_principles.problem: Many users compete for scarce multi-node GPU capacity for long-running jobs.
truths: Batch jobs need all resources together.
Long jobs will fail at some point.

analogy.title: An airport slot system
analogy.story: Airlines request slots, the tower allocates runways fairly, and diverted flights resume from where they landed.
analogy.breaks: Flights can't resume mid-air; Slurm jobs resume mid-training from checkpoints.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Design for interruption from day one.

check.q: Which daemon makes scheduling decisions in Slurm?

aido-model-quantization.core: Quantization stores and computes with fewer bits by mapping float ranges onto integer grids (scale + zero-point). Calibration sets activation ranges, PTQ or QAT trade effort for accuracy, hardware kernels turn smaller numbers into speed, and mixed precision protects sensitive layers.

first_principles.problem: Full-precision models are too big and slow to serve affordably.

analogy.title: Compressing a photo for the web
analogy.story: Fewer colours and bits, nearly the same picture, loading much faster, with care for faces and fine details.
analogy.breaks: Image artefacts are visible; model degradation must be measured with evals.
